results.corrected_extracted: Second-hand: lifetime dependence among people who had ever tried cannabis estimated at 9% in 1992 (Anthony, Warner and Kessler, 1994), against tobacco 32%, heroin 23%, cocaine 17% and alcohol 15%; more recent nationally representative US data suggesting about 30% of people who use cannabis may develop a use disorder (Hasin et al., 2015), with no diagnostic system, time frame or denominator given, which the authors suggest, without data, may reflect higher potency, legal change and acceptance. The abstract gives about 10% of 193 million people who use cannabis worldwide, without a citation, and the introduction 1 in 10 people who use it regularly, cited to the UN World Drug Report 2020 (ref 1), on past-year or regular-use denominators rather than ever use (the card notes the change of denominator).
results.note: The abstract carries no citation: its ~10% of 193 million is uncited, while the body's UN figure (ref 1) is 192 million past-year users (introduction and Prevalence, 1st paragraphs). Other numbers, wording and refs 1, 30, 32 confirmed.

Recounted from Table 1 (50 rows): 23,518 people; sizes times prevalences 6,469.95 (27.5%); unweighted mean 47.548%; crude 18.58%, 51.52%, 82.16% (15/28/7 cohorts; 17,475/5,684/359 people); CUD criteria DSM-III-R 8, DSM-IV 38, DSM-5 4.

Introduction paragraph 2 lists the seven symptoms 'within 7 days of reduced cannabis use'; Importance: 'on cessation of heavy and prolonged cannabis use'; Statistical Analysis paragraph 1: lowest threshold where studies used multiple cut points.

results.corrected_extracted: DSM-5 withdrawal in the Primer's words: three or more signs within 1 week of cessation (irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; decreased appetite or weight loss; restlessness; depressed mood; at least one physical symptom causing severe discomfort, such as abdominal pain, shakiness, sweating, fever, chills or headache), which must cause clinically severe distress or impairment (the Primer's wording; reduced use is not mentioned). Many of these symptoms also occur in other substance withdrawal or in other mental disorders. Second-hand: symptoms typically begin 24-48 hours after stopping, peak within the first week and last 1-2 weeks (Budney et al., 2003); 12% of people who use frequently had DSM-5 withdrawal in the past 12 months in a US national sample (Livne et al., 2019). In Management, figures cited to Livne et al. and Bahji et al. together (refs 177 and 203) are relabelled as 12-17% in the general population of people who use cannabis and as 54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients with a use disorder seeking treatment reporting clinically severe withdrawal. Without medical or psychiatric comorbidity, withdrawal is said not to pose serious risks, with most people needing only supportive care, in a sentence that cites no source.
results.note: Both Management sentences cite refs 177 (Livne et al.) and 203 (Bahji et al.), not Bahji alone; the 12% matches Livne's frequent-use figure. Diagnostic systems paragraph 3, refs 176-177 and the uncited no-serious-risk sentence confirmed.

Differential diagnosis paragraph 3 and refs 188-190 as stated ('almost all patients with CHS are heavy weekly cannabis users'). The Primer's reference list gives no article type for Chocron et al. (2019), so 'clinical review' is not checkable here.

results.corrected_extracted: Against placebo: at least 30% pain reduction OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00), 8 trials, 1370 patients, I2 48%, GRADE moderate (abstract: 37% vs 31%); the one smoked-THC trial OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48), the other 7 nabiximols; neuropathic pain OR 1.38 (0.93 to 2.03), 6 trials. Nabiximols: pain NRS WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11) on 0 to 10, 6 trials, 948 patients, I2 59%, moderate; Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16), 3 trials; Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 (-7.32 to -0.47) on 0 to 100, 5 trials; global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59), 6 trials (5 nabiximols and 1 nabilone by Table 2; the text names nabiximols), 267 patients, I2 68%, low; EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02), 3 trials. Sensitivity analyses adding crossover trials were reported as consistent. The abstract's percentages are not derived in the text or tables; they equal the crude event totals of Figure 2 (see the Figure 2 anchor); the cancer-pain subgroup estimate is misprinted and not used.
results.note: Table 2's global-impression row lists nabiximols (5) and nabilone (1), though the text says nabiximols. All other text, Table 2 and abstract figures confirmed; the cancer-pain OR equals the overall. Figure 2 equality not viewable (see Figure 2 anchor).

Spasticity paragraph, Table 2 spasticity rows, the abstract and the article's correction note (13 July 2015, Ashworth estimate) all match; Table 2 prints -0.11 first, beside Nabiximols (4) listed first.

results.corrected_extracted: Preterm birth (before 37 weeks by the WHO definition, which the Methods say 7 of the 8 included studies used, while the Results count 9 studies), 9 studies: random-effects pooled OR 1.29 (95% CI 0.80 to 2.08; I2 85%), not statistically significant. The text's lists of positive and null studies overlap and omit one study, so the count of positive studies cannot be checked (study card reporting issue). Small for gestational age was assessed in 2 studies (1 with higher odds, 1 null) and not pooled; the article gives no reason.
results.note: Growth parameters confirms 9 studies, pOR 1.29 (0.80-2.08), I2 85%; ref 19 is in both lists, 28 in neither. No reason is given for not pooling the two SGA studies. Figure 1 (flow chart) not viewable; not needed.

Discussion paragraphs 6-7 (of 8) and box bullets 3-5 as stated: 'well established' that tobacco and heavy alcohol use increase LBW, PTB and SGA; self-report 'may have underestimated' use; few outcomes standardised or defined.
